newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Refocus on data after FOMC.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Refocus on data after FOMC.

text.p: The U.S. credit market will turn its focus back to the data front on Wednesday, even as it continues to digest the Federal Reserve's decision to leave short-term interest rates unchanged.
The Treasury's scheduled sale of $18.25 billion in two-year notes is also expected to garner attention on a day which promises little in the way of price movement, analysts said.

"I think probably next week's data will play a larger role than this week's, but there's always a chance of some market reaction to existing home sales," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities.

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) will release existing home sales for the month of August at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. U.S. economists in a Reuters survey are calling for 4.09 million annualized units in August versus 4.14 million in July.
Bostjancic said plateauing mortgage applications and already high home sales levels argue for a decline.
However, any gains are likely to be limited by strong technical resistance at the 109-even level on the December T-bond futures contract, analysts said.
And the Fed's decision to hold rates steady on Tuesday is no guarantee that the Treasury's two-year note auction will go well.

"I think people are still thinking the Fed will move at sometime later this year," said Damon Whelchel, treasury market analyst at MMS International. "Because of that I don't think the two-year note auction is going to be a shoo-in."
Analysts also said the Treasury yield curve could steepen further in the aftermath of Tuesday's rate decision as concerns the Fed is behind the inflation curve mount.
The spread between the two-year note and the thirty-year bond closed at 85 basis points on Tuesday, up from 78 basis points at Monday's close.
"(Steepening) is probably in the market sentiment right now," said UBS's Bostjancic.
In her view however, the Fed's inaction on Tuesday was consistent with a slowing economy in which inflation pressures are largely contained.
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond closed up 14/32 at 97-01/32 to yield 6.99 percent. The federal funds rate is expected to open between 5-3/8 and 5-1/2 percent.
